questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: Prolonged vomiting from pyloric obstruction produces:
options: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
questions.concept: Loss of gastric acid depletes hydrogen and chloride; the kidney retains sodium and bicarbonate and excretes hydrogen and potassium, producing paradoxical aciduria. Correction is with normal saline and potassium.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: Large-volume resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride can produce:
questions.concept: Normal saline has a chloride concentration of 154 mmol/L, well above plasma, so large volumes cause a dilutional hyperchloraemic normal anion gap acidosis. Balanced crystalloids such as Ringer lactate avoid this.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: The daily maintenance requirement of sodium in an adult is approximately:
options: 1 to 2 mmol per kg per day
questions.concept: Adults need about 1 to 2 mmol/kg/day of sodium, 1 mmol/kg/day of potassium and 25 to 30 mL/kg/day of water, adjusted for losses from drains, fistulae, fever and third-space sequestration.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: The preferred route of nutritional support in a surgical patient with a functioning gut is:
questions.concept: If the gut works, use it: enteral feeding maintains mucosal integrity, reduces bacterial translocation and septic complications, and is cheaper and safer than parenteral nutrition.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: The most serious complication of central venous total parenteral nutrition is:
questions.concept: Line sepsis is the most serious complication, requiring strict aseptic technique and a dedicated lumen. Metabolic complications include hyperglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance, hepatic steatosis and refeeding syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: Third-space loss in a surgical patient refers to:
options: Sequestration of extracellular fluid into the bowel lumen, peritoneum or interstitium where it is non-functional
questions.concept: Fluid shifted into the interstitium, gut lumen or peritoneal cavity after surgery, peritonitis or obstruction is lost from the circulation despite remaining in the body, so it must be replaced with isotonic crystalloid.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: The best simple bedside indicator of adequate resuscitation in a surgical patient is:
options: Urine output of at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour
questions.concept: Urine output reflects renal perfusion and is a practical continuous marker, supported by heart rate, capillary refill, mental state and lactate clearance. Blood pressure is maintained until late by compensation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: Refeeding syndrome in a malnourished surgical patient is characterised by:
options: Hypophosphataemia with hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia after reintroduction of feeding
questions.concept: Carbohydrate-driven insulin release shifts phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly, risking arrhythmia and cardiac failure. Feeding is started at reduced calories with thiamine and electrolyte monitoring.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is treated first with:
options: Intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilise the myocardium
questions.concept: Calcium does not lower potassium but immediately antagonises its membrane effect and prevents arrhythmia, buying time for insulin-dextrose, salbutamol and bicarbonate to shift potassium intracellularly, and for dialysis or resins to remove it.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion after surgery produces:
options: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and high urinary sodium
questions.concept: SIADH gives hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine, urinary sodium above 40 mmol/L and clinical euvolaemia, with low serum osmolality. Fluid restriction is first-line; correction must be gradual.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The commonest cause of a fatal acute haemolytic transfusion reaction is:
options: ABO incompatibility from clerical error in patient identification
questions.concept: Misidentification of patient or sample leading to ABO-incompatible transfusion causes complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis with fever, loin pain, hypotension, haemoglobinuria and disseminated intravascular coagulation. The transfusion must be stopped immediately.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Massive blood transfusion is commonly complicated by:
options: Hypothermia, hypocalcaemia from citrate, hyperkalaemia and dilutional coagulopathy
questions.concept: Stored blood is cold, citrated and potassium-rich with no functional platelets or labile clotting factors, so massive transfusion requires warming, calcium supplementation and balanced replacement with plasma and platelets.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The commonest transfusion reaction overall is:
options: Febrile non-haemolytic reaction from leucocyte antibodies and cytokines
questions.concept: Febrile non-haemolytic reactions from donor leucocytes and accumulated cytokines are the commonest, prevented by leucodepletion. Haemolysis must always be excluded before attributing fever to this benign cause.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Fresh frozen plasma is indicated for:
options: Replacement of multiple coagulation factor deficiencies with active bleeding or before an urgent procedure
questions.concept: FFP contains all clotting factors and is used in coagulopathy of liver disease, disseminated intravascular coagulation, massive transfusion and urgent warfarin reversal when concentrates are unavailable. It should not be used as a volume expander.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Cryoprecipitate is particularly rich in:
options: Fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII
questions.concept: Cryoprecipitate is the preferred fibrinogen source in disseminated intravascular coagulation and massive haemorrhage when fibrinogen falls below about 1.5 g/L, and also supplies factor VIII, vWF and factor XIII.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) presents as:
options: Acute non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema within six hours of transfusion
questions.concept: Donor antibodies against recipient leucocytes cause acute hypoxaemia with bilateral infiltrates and normal filling pressures within 6 hours, distinguishing it from circulatory overload. Treatment is supportive and it is a leading cause of transfusion mortality.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Anaphylactic transfusion reactions occur classically in recipients with:
questions.concept: IgA-deficient recipients with anti-IgA antibodies react anaphylactically to IgA in donor plasma, and require washed red cells or IgA-deficient products for future transfusions.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The universal donor for packed red cells and universal donor for plasma are respectively:
questions.concept: O negative red cells lack A, B and D antigens so can be given to anyone, while AB plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies making it the universal plasma donor - the relationship is inverted between components.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Tranexamic acid reduces surgical bleeding by:
options: Inhibiting plasminogen activation and thereby fibrinolysis
questions.concept: Tranexamic acid is a lysine analogue that blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin, stabilising clot. It reduces mortality in trauma haemorrhage when given within three hours (CRASH-2) and in postpartum haemorrhage.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Autologous blood transfusion has the principal advantage of:
questions.concept: Predeposit autologous donation, acute normovolaemic haemodilution and intraoperative cell salvage avoid immunological reactions and infection transmission, though cell salvage is avoided where the field is contaminated by infection or malignancy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The commonest cause of portal hypertension in India is:
questions.concept: Cirrhosis is the commonest cause overall, giving intrahepatic sinusoidal obstruction. Extrahepatic portal vein obstruction is an important cause of variceal bleeding in Indian children with preserved liver function.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The first-line treatment for acute variceal bleeding is:
options: Resuscitation with endoscopic variceal band ligation and a vasoactive drug such as terlipressin or octreotide
questions.concept: Resuscitation, vasoactive drugs, antibiotic prophylaxis and urgent endoscopic band ligation control most bleeds. Balloon tamponade is a temporary bridge, and TIPS is used for failure of endoscopic control.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Primary prophylaxis against variceal bleeding in a cirrhotic with large varices uses:
options: Non-selective beta blockers such as propranolol or carvedilol, or band ligation
questions.concept: Non-selective beta blockade reduces portal pressure by splanchnic vasoconstriction and reduced cardiac output; band ligation is an alternative for those intolerant. Selective beta-1 blockers do not work because the splanchnic beta-2 effect is required.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The Child-Pugh score assesses all EXCEPT:
questions.concept: Child-Pugh uses bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time or INR, ascites and encephalopathy. Creatinine features in the MELD score, which also uses bilirubin and INR and is used for transplant prioritisation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A liver abscess in India is most commonly:
options: Amoebic, solitary and in the right lobe
questions.concept: Amoebic liver abscess from Entamoeba histolytica is usually solitary in the right lobe with anchovy-sauce pus that is sterile on culture. Metronidazole is curative, with aspiration for large or left-lobe abscesses or impending rupture.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: In hydatid cyst of the liver, the danger of percutaneous aspiration is:
options: Anaphylaxis and dissemination of daughter cysts
questions.concept: Spillage of cyst contents can cause anaphylactic shock and peritoneal seeding. If PAIR is performed it is done under albendazole cover with a scolicidal agent; surgery involves careful removal without spillage.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The most feared long-term complication after splenectomy is:
options: Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection by encapsulated organisms
questions.concept: Loss of splenic macrophages and opsonisation predisposes to fulminant sepsis from pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus influenzae. Vaccination at least two weeks before elective splenectomy and prophylactic penicillin are essential.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which vaccines must be given before elective splenectomy?
options: Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b
questions.concept: Vaccination against the three encapsulated organisms is given at least two weeks preoperatively for optimal response, or two weeks postoperatively after emergency splenectomy, with annual influenza vaccine and antibiotic prophylaxis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Alpha-fetoprotein is most useful as a tumour marker in:
options: Hepatocellular carcinoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumours
questions.concept: AFP is raised in hepatocellular carcinoma, used with ultrasound for surveillance in cirrhosis, and in yolk sac and embryonal elements of testicular tumours. Pure seminoma does not raise AFP.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Budd-Chiari syndrome is caused by:
options: Hepatic venous outflow obstruction, presenting with hepatomegaly, ascites and abdominal pain
questions.concept: Occlusion of the hepatic veins or suprahepatic inferior vena cava, often from a myeloproliferative disorder or thrombophilia, causes tender hepatomegaly with intractable ascites and caudate lobe hypertrophy from its separate venous drainage.
